From the Indian market point of view, the airline sees cargo and MRO businesses as strong segments.With around 18,000 aircraft backlogged at manufacturers, airlines are extending leases, and that means more heavy checks, he said, adding that no Indian airline sends aircraft to Malaysia Airlines' MRO arm today. But he sees it as a chance, since the group works on both Boeing and Airbus. When told, India has long complained about losing maintenance business abroad, his answer was diplomatic: "To me, the cake is so big that everyone can have a portion. " Cargo and MRO are two of the group's six non-airline businesses, along with loyalty, catering, ground handling and a training academy.Malaysia Airlines has a codeshare with IndiGo on six Indian domestic points and a joint business agreement with Singapore Airlines. It is also a Oneworld member, though that alliance has no Indian carrier. The CEO did not have passenger numbers for the IndiGo tie-up. “In terms of the number, it is steadily improving. It is not there yet, but we need it, we want it to be much better.”IndiGo's push into long-haul does not worry him unduly. Thirty or forty years ago, he notes, Southeast Asia and India had only six or seven airlines, and now there are more than 50. "Competition is stiff, but the market has grown a lot." He expects the Asia-Pacific region to grow six to seven per cent a year for the next 20 years, against about four per cent globally. "Of course, it is a concern to us. Even though the market is big, we have to be very smart. "Technology, too, is on his list, as is with most airline CEOs. About 75 per cent of customers now start their search on Google or an AI tool, and about 20 percent of those convert into a ticket, he said. Malaysia Airlines runs 49 AI platforms across its operations, from flight planning to disruption management. Citing an example, he talks about rebooking disrupted passengers, where the system can use customer data to decide who goes on which flight, such as sending someone bound for London directly rather than through KL.
Article Summary: Nasaruddin A Bakar is the CEO of Malaysia Aviation Group. He took charge just before before the West Asia crisis began. He talks to the Times of India about running a thin-margin airline through a crisis. He also talks about why India matters more than ever and what happens when the visa-free window closes.

Article Title: Major crackdown on Green Cards: What is PERM program & which IT firms has US suspended
Article Text:
Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing it of laying off 6,000 American workers in 2025

Microsoft Adobe Cognizant Infosys Tata Wipro HCL Capgemini

What is PERM visa and how does it work?

The US has suspended eight major technology companies, including Microsoft, Tata, Infosys and Wipro, from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, in a major crackdown on the use of foreign workers for jobs that the government says could be filled by Americans. The move was announced by Vice President JD Vance, Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling and Attorney General Todd Blanche under the US Anti-Fraud Task Force.The Department of Labour said it would not accept new or process pending PERM applications involving the companies. Sonderling said the firms alone had requested almost three million foreign workers since 2009, securing more than 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications.Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing it of laying off 6,000 American workers in 2025 while obtaining more than 6,000 H-1B approvals and filing 3,682 PERM applications. "Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 after certifying that it could not find qualified American employees," Vance said.Which IT firms are suspended from PERM programme:Sonderling said the suspensions covered some of the world's largest IT outsourcing companies.He said Microsoft and Adobe were being suspended due to multiple active federal investigations, while the other firms were also targeted as part of the broader crackdown.Indian professionals account for more than 70% of approved H-1B petitions annually, making the move particularly significant for Indian technology workers seeking permanent residency in the US.PERM, or Permanent Labour Certification, is not itself a visa. It is a labour certification process administered by the US Department of Labour that is required for most employment-based green card applications.Under the system, a US employer must establish that there are not enough qualified, willing and available American workers for a particular job, and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.The process generally begins with the employer identifying a permanent, full-time position and determining its minimum requirements and duties. The employer then obtains a prevailing wage determination from the Department of Labour.The employer must also complete the required recruitment and notification process to demonstrate that it has sought qualified US workers. After completing these steps, it submits the PERM application to the Department of Labour, usually through the online FLAG system. If the labour certification is approved, the employer can use it as a step towards filing the relevant employment-based immigrant petition with US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).
Article Summary: The US has suspended eight major technology companies, including Microsoft, Tata, Infosys and Wipro. The move was announced by Vice President JD Vance, Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling and Attorney General Todd Blanche. The Department of Labour said it would not accept new or process pending PERM applications involving the companies.

Article Title: US visa chaos: Tata, Wipro among IT firms suspended from PERM scheme; what it means
Article Text:
The PERM programme is a key step in the employment-based green card process

What is the PERM programme

How PERM was meant to protect US workers

NEW DELHI: The Trump administration has stepped up its crackdown on the US immigration system, suspending major technology companies including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, Capgemini and HCL from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme amid allegations of abuse of H-1B visas and the employment of foreign workers.US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of laying off thousands of American workers while simultaneously benefiting from thousands of H-1B visas and green cards. The administration has also put nine universities under investigation over alleged misuse of visa-related programmes, adding to growing uncertainty for foreign workers and international students in the US.Announcing Microsoft's suspension from the PERM programme, Vance said the company had laid off 6,000 American workers while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards."There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft."“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said at a White House news conference.Vance also accused companies of using foreign workers to undercut American employees, saying: "This is a fundamental INSULT to the American worker and to the American way of life. We CANNOT allow visa programs that were designed to ensure that American corporations had access to the best and the brightest, to use them to undercut the wages of American workers!"The Permanent Labour Certification programme, or PERM, is a Department of Labour process that allows US employers to seek certification to permanently employ foreign workers.Under the process, employers generally have to demonstrate that there are not enough able, willing, qualified and available US workers for the job and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed American workers.Once the labour certification is approved by the Department of Labour, the employer can proceed with an immigrant petition to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, generally through Form I-140.For H-1B workers, PERM can therefore form an important step in the employment-based green card process. Suspending a company's access to the programme can make it harder for the company to sponsor eligible foreign workers for permanent residence.The PERM programme is designed to ensure that American workers are not disadvantaged when employers seek to hire foreign workers for permanent jobs. Before sponsoring a foreign worker for a green card, an employer generally has to demonstrate that there are not enough qualified, willing and available US workers for the position and that hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed Americans.The concern for US authorities arises when employers manipulate or bypass this labour-market test. Fraudulent recruitment can make it appear that no suitable American worker is available when, in reality, qualified US workers may have been discouraged from applying or effectively excluded from consideration. The Department of Labor's inspector general has identified vulnerabilities in the PERM system, including concerns over fraudulent applications, inadequate supporting documentation and weaknesses in post-certification enforcement.Wages are another concern. Employers are required to meet prevailing wage requirements, which are intended to prevent foreign-worker hiring from depressing wages for American workers in comparable jobs. If employers circumvent these requirements or use arrangements that effectively reduce the foreign worker's compensation, the government says the system can undermine the safeguards built into PERM.The administration's latest moves have also extended beyond companies. The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $70,000 fee for international students participating in the Optional Practical Training programme, which allows eligible foreign students to work in jobs related to their studies.
Article Summary: The Trump administration has stepped up its crackdown on the US immigration system. It has suspended major technology companies including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, Capgemini and HCL from the Permanent Labour Certification programme. The administration has also put nine universities under investigation over alleged misuse of visa-related programmes.

Article Title: AI could turn fresh finance hires into managers from day one: Goldman Sachs
Article Text:
AI could make young finance hires managers from day one

What will young hires do

Traditional career ladder may change

Banks may need fewer fresh graduates

As artificial intelligence advances, young finance professionals may no longer have to spend years waiting for their first management role.With AI taking on more work, new hires could find themselves managing AI agents from the start of their careers, according to Goldman Sachs executive Kevin Sneader.Sneader, who leads Goldman Sachs Group Inc.’s business in Asia Pacific outside Japan, said that the shift could also raise questions about the future role of middle managers, who have traditionally taken on management responsibilities after years of experience.“When our young folks now start work, they’re managing agents,” Sneader said on Thursday at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore. “They have to make the most of this virtual army that they’ve now got.”Bloomberg Previous generations often spent years in their jobs before getting the opportunity to manage anyone. But as AI changes the way work is done, management responsibilities could move closer to the front line.“That management task no longer sits with the middle manager; it sits with the front line,” Sneader said. “We don’t quite know what’s going to happen to that group.”Sneader said re-deploying existing managers would be the “generational challenge for many, many segments”.The comments point to a possible change in the traditional banking career path, where junior employees spend years working on analysis and preparatory tasks before moving into management roles.Rather than focusing on mass job losses from AI, Sneader and other panellists discussing AI and finance focused on how jobs and responsibilities could be reshaped.Sandra Peterson, an operating partner at investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice, said the traditional career ladder in professional services may not survive in the same form.“It used to be that professional service firms were pyramids,” she said. “You’d show up, and you know, you march your way through, and if you survived, you got to the next level, the next level, the next level.”With AI doing much of the grunt work, Peterson said it was unclear whether firms would need as many entry-level positions.Singapore’s financial regulator is also seeing changes in how jobs could be organised. Chia Der Jiun, managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said operations staff would need to become managers and supervisors of AI agents.Banks would also need fewer fresh graduates for analysis and preparatory work, he said.Singapore has been preparing for these changes by training bank staff in AI skills and working with universities to ensure its graduates are ready for the new world, Chia said.For young people, Sneader said the opportunities could extend beyond finding a job in finance.“There’s never been a better time to be an entrepreneur to create something,” he said, noting that fewer resources are needed to start a business nowadays.“That’s quite an exciting part of the future when we’re all spending too much time, perhaps worrying about the old world.
Article Summary: New hires could find themselves managing AI agents from the start of their careers, says Goldman Sachs executive Kevin Sneader. Previous generations often spent years in their jobs before getting the opportunity to manage anyone. Sneader said re-deploying existing managers would be the “generational challenge for many, many segments”

Article Title: Russia eyes return to Europe's gas market despite sanctions, Ukraine war: Report
Article Text:
Russia aims to reach Europe’s gas market through Nord Stream pipeline (Representational image)

Nord Stream back on the table

Restarting gas flows won't be easy

Germany split over Russian gas

Who owns Nord Stream?

Lukoil assets also in focus

Russia may be looking to turn the gas taps to Europe back on, with talks under way over bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that once carried Russian gas to Germany.According to five people familiar with the matter, the discussions involve US Special Envoy Jared Kushner and Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin.Kushner, who has been trying to broker a truce between Russia and Ukraine, sees business deals as central to restoring peace. A potential Nord Stream deal could allow US investors to profit from energy flows to Europe once the war ends.Kushner and Dmitriev have met in Moscow and New York in recent weeks. Two sources told Reuters that Nord Stream remains on the agenda, although not much details are available about the discussions.Dmitriev, who has been pushing for Russian gas sales to Germany to resume, met representatives of the US energy and treasury departments last month, to discuss potential US-Russia energy initiatives.A White House official said that any deals would have to be negotiated with the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and Treasury and must benefit US taxpayers and companies."Any deals will have to be negotiated by Russia with DFC (US International Development Finance Corporation) and Treasury and must benefit United States taxpayers and companies," the official said.The official also said there had been "no Nord Stream discussions recently".A return of Russian gas to Germany still faces several hurdles. The Nord Stream pipelines are sanctioned by the US and the EU, making any restart illegal.A US official said a deal was unlikely in the medium term because of the obstacles involved. US President Donald Trump could waive or soften US sanctions, but that would become harder if Democrats win control of Congress in next month's midterm elections.Germany and other European countries are also expected to oppose reopening Nord Stream. They are spending billions of euros rebuilding their military to defend themselves from Russia.A spokeswoman for Germany's economy and energy ministry said Nord Stream and Russian gas were sanctioned in Europe and that Germany had found alternatives. She said reopening the pipelines would require government approval and was not desired.Before Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Germany bought more than half of its gas from Russia through the two Nord Stream pipelines. They were mothballed after Moscow throttled supplies to Europe and were blown up in a series of underwater explosions in September 2022.The idea of bringing Russian gas back to Germany has also divided opinion within the country.Germany's coalition government is opposed to restarting the pipeline, while Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country's most popular political party, wants to reopen it. Dmitriev is due to meet AfD leadership early next year to discuss selling Russian gas again.Poland is also watching the discussions but remains firmly opposed to reopening the pipeline, according to one person familiar with the government's thinking. Poland and the Baltic states are particularly vulnerable to Russia and reject energy ties.The talks are taking place against a backdrop of deep European mistrust of Russia's motives. Earlier this year, the heads of five European spy agencies told Reuters that Russia did not want to end the war quickly and was using US talks to push for business deals instead.Relations between Russia and Germany, which is among the biggest providers of military support to Ukraine, have hit a low ebb. Officials in Berlin have accused Russia of mounting a systematic campaign of hybrid attacks.Some German lawmakers say business deals would bolster Moscow as it pursues war with Ukraine."This threatens to be a dirty deal that will cost Europe dearly," said Michael Kellner, a lawmaker who was in charge of German energy policy in the aftermath of the Ukraine invasion."Americans and Russians will share the profits," he said.Ownership could be another hurdle for any US investment in Nord Stream.Russian state energy giant Gazprom owns 51% of the company. Another 31% is split between two German entities, while the remaining stake is held by a French and a Dutch firm.The two German shareholders want to retain their stakes to maintain German influence if Gazprom sells its share, another person familiar with the matter said.Days after the Moscow meetings, Kushner said in Kyiv that he had spoken to European counterparts about how the war had pushed up energy prices. He advocated "prosperity agreements" to encourage peace and give "leaders ... something to look forward to".Kushner and Dmitriev have also discussed the possible sale of businesses owned by Russian energy company Lukoil, including oil refineries and petrol stations in Europe and elsewhere, two people familiar with the matter said.Under the proposal, a consortium involving the DFC and investors from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates would buy the assets, while US authorities would lift sanctions, the people said."On Lukoil, Steve (Witkoff) and Jared (Kushner) worked with DFC to negotiate a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States," a White House official said.
Article Summary: Talks under way over bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that once carried Russian gas to Germany. US Special Envoy Jared Kushner sees business deals as central to restoring peace. A potential Nord Stream deal could allow US investors to profit from energy flows to Europe.

Article Title: US mortgage rates jump to 7.49%, hit highest level in nearly 3 years
Article Text:
US mortgage rate climbs to three year high

US mortgage rates have soared to their highest level in nearly three years, with the sharp rise in borrowing costs adding to pressure on the housing market as Americans head towards November 3 elections.The average rate for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose 19 basis points to 7.49% in the week ended October 2, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) said, as cited by Reuters. This spike pushed rates to the highest level since November 2023, hitting demand for home loans.Mortgage applications dropped 4.2% last week from the previous week, while refinancing applications fell sharply. Overall application volumes are now at their lowest since February 2025 and have declined nearly 50% since January."Very few homeowners have an incentive to refinance at these rates, and the jump in borrowing costs has caused many potential borrowers to step back from the purchase market," Joel Kan, the MBA’s deputy chief economist told Reuters.Mortgage rates have closely followed movements in the yield on 10-year US treasury notes. Earlier this week, the yield topped 5.3%, reaching a 24-year high, with concerns over inflationary pressures from soaring oil prices and data showing stronger US economic growth driving the rise.Home borrowing rates are up about 1.4 percentage points since joint US-Israeli strikes against Iran began in late February, tracking a similar increase in the 10-year treasury yield.The increase comes at a politically sensitive time, with the US mid-term elections just four weeks away. The cost of living was the top issue among Americans in deciding how they would vote, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday. At the same time, US President Donald Trump's approval rating stood at a record low of 32%.Inflation has also risen, reaching 3.4% in August on a measure targeted by the Federal Reserve at 2%.Fed policymakers have signalled that they expect another interest-rate increase by the end of the year following the rate hike in September. Markets are currently betting that policymakers will not raise rates at the next meeting at the end of October.The latest increase in mortgage rates comes as affordability remains under pressure for buyers, while the decline in loan applications points to weaker activity in the mortgage market.
Article Summary: US mortgage rates have soared to their highest level in nearly three years. The average rate for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose 19 basis points to 7.49%. This spike pushed rates to the highest level since November 2023, hitting demand for home loans.

Article Title: Oil remains beyond $100 per barrel as Middle East supply concerns persist
Article Text:
Crude oil prices continue to rally

Oil prices inched higher on Thursday as concerns over supply from the Middle East intensified amid a rise in attacks on vessels in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.Brent crude was trading at $101.50 a barrel, up $1.32 or 1.32%, while WTI crude stood at $89.28, gaining $1 or 1.13%.The latest gains come despite a fall in prices in the previous session, when the International Energy Agency agreed to speed up the release of oil stocks and give priority to diesel supplies. The plan, launched in March, is aimed at dealing with record fuel prices and supply disruptions linked to the Iran war.Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has become a growing concern as the US-Israeli conflict with Iran enters its eighth month. Before the war, the route handled shipments equivalent to about 20% of global oil and fuel supplies.The pressure on shipping has increased even as Gulf producers raise exports. Tanker attacks through the Strait reached their highest level last week for any week since the Iran war began, leaving crude shipments facing higher costs and greater risks for cargoes and crew.A tanker north of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles in the latest attack, causing casualties, the United Kingdom maritime trade operations agency said on Wednesday.Supply concerns were accompanied by signs of tighter US inventories. According to Reuters, American crude stocks fell by 3.2 million barrels in the week ended October 2 to 424.1 million barrels, according to the Energy Information Administration. The decline was larger than the 1.7 million-barrel fall analysts had expected in a Reuters poll.Diesel and jet fuel inventories also declined, with distillate fuel stocks falling by 42,000 barrels to 105.14 million barrels. Those inventories remained below their levels for this period of the year over the past five years.Oil markets have remained unsettled for more than seven months since the Middle East conflict began. Even with the latest increase, prices are still below the $126 a barrel level reached earlier in the crisis.
Article Summary: Brent crude was trading at $101.50 a barrel, up $1.32 or 1.32%. WTI crude stood at $89.28, gaining $1 or1.13%. The latest gains come despite a fall in prices in the previous session.

Article Title: Iraq’s dinar takes a hit as official rate resets, market rate crosses 1,700
Article Text:
Iraq devalues its currency

Iraq’s dinar has taken a step down against the US dollar, with the country officially resetting its exchange rate from around 1,300 dinars to 1,500 dinars per dollar. But in the market, the dollar is already fetching more than 1,700 dinars.The new official rate was decided at a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday night, according to Iraq’s central bank, which said the move was made “to meet the relevant financial, economic and monetary requirements.”The previous official exchange rate had been set in 2023. In practice, however, Iraq has always had a difference between the official rate and the rate used by exchange shops. That gap had widened in recent months, with the unofficial rate crossing 1,600 dinars to the dollar even before the official devaluation.After the new official rate was announced, the market rate climbed further to more than 1,700 dinars per dollar.The widening gap has come amid the US-Iran war, which has at times spilled over into Iraq, and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Iraq’s economy relies heavily on oil exports, most of which were shipped through the strait before the war. Since the war began, Iraq has shifted to sending oil overland through Syria for export, a route that is more expensive and less efficient.Under the new official rate, Iraq’s Finance Ministry will sell dollars at 1,500 dinars per dollar, while consumers buying dollars from banks will pay 1,520 dinars per dollar.
Article Summary: Iraq devalues its dinar against the US dollar. The new official rate is 1,500 dinars per dollar. But in the market, the dollar is already fetching more than 1,700 dinars. The widening gap has come amid the US-Iran war and disruptions to shipping.

Article Title: Amazon Prime becomes 'permanent home' for Emmy Awards as 'Wheel Deal' system ends
Article Text:
Emmys shift from 'Wheel Deal' to Amazon Prime

The Emmys are leaving their decades-old broadcast TV rotation behind, with Amazon’s Prime Video set to become the awards show’s exclusive global streaming home from 2027.The Television Academy and Amazon announced a six-year agreement on Tuesday that will make the ceremony available live and free to audiences in more than 240 countries and territories. Furthermore, viewers will not need a Prime Video subscription to watch the show.The ceremony will continue to take place in September, with Prime Video’s rights beginning with the 2027 edition. NBC, owned by Comcast, aired this year’s ceremony on September 14.The deal brings an end to the “Wheel Deal” system under which ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC took turns broadcasting the Emmys. The arrangement has been in place since at least 1994, with the latest eight-year contract expiring this year.Prime Video has been named the “permanent home” of the Emmys in the announcement, marking a departure from the awards show’s long-running practice of moving between the four US broadcast networks.“Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share,” Television Academy chair Cris Abrego said in a statement.“Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year,” he said.The financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed.The move comes as streaming services take a larger role in live television, while traditional broadcast and cable networks face increasing competition as viewing habits shift towards streaming subscriptions. Major entertainment and sports events have increasingly moved to or added streaming platforms, including events whose rights were previously held exclusively by traditional networks.The Emmys' move is also part of a wider shift among major US awards shows. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced in December 2025 that Alphabet’s YouTube and YouTube TV would take over media rights to the Oscars from ABC in 2029. Netflix has exclusively aired the SAG Awards since 2024.For Amazon, the agreement adds a major live entertainment event to Prime Video’s existing offering of original films and television programmes, sports and other streaming partnerships.First held in 1949, the Emmy Awards recognise achievements in television acting, production and writing, among other categories. The ceremony has traditionally been a major promotional and cultural event for the US television industry.
Article Summary: The Emmys are leaving their decades-old broadcast TV rotation behind. Amazon's Prime Video will become the awards show's exclusive global streaming home from 2027. The deal brings an end to the “Wheel Deal’ system under which ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC took turns broadcasting the Emmys.

Article Title: Brent crosses $101 as Saudi attacks, US storm add to oil supply concerns
Article Text:
Brent crosses $101 once again

Oil prices rose more than 1% on Wednesday, with Brent crude crossing the $101-a-barrel mark as fresh supply risks outweighed rising optimism due to increased Middle East crude supplies.WTI crude rose 1.05% to $90.38 a barrel, while Brent crude gained 1.02% to $101.60 as supply concerns emerged in Saudi Arabia and the US oil and refining sector.The latest concerns came from both sides of the global oil supply chain. According to US forecasters, a storm developing in the Gulf of Mexico is expected to become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days and is likely to affect oil and gas facilities.The areas in the storm's path account for 15% of US crude production and 5% of the country's natural gas production. Six refineries could also be affected. Refineries located in US Gulf states represent about 50% of the country's total refining capacity of 18.2 million barrels per day (bpd).The prospect of disruption has emerged even as oil supplies from the Middle East have increased. Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman on Tuesday said that supply had been rising, with the East-West pipeline reaching 5.8 million barrels a day.The head of Vitol said that around 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million bpd of refined products had been shipped out of the Middle East by tankers over the previous seven to 10 days.US inventory data, however, offered a mixed picture. According to market sources citing by Reuters, crude and gasoline inventories declined last week, while distillate stocks increased marginally. US crude inventories fell by 2.09 million barrels in the week ended October 2.Meanwhile, tensions around Saudi Arabia have added another risk to regional supply. The Saudi aviation authority said airports in Jazan and Najran were attacked twice on Monday evening as hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis escalated.The attacks came as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pursued a major offensive to regain territory from the Houthis after weeks of rebel advances. Saudi Arabia has increased airstrikes in support of the campaign.Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at X Analysts in Sydney, said the attacks and refinery outages could continue to support higher oil prices.“Attacks and refinery outages are likely to keep the cracks elevated and scarcity will transmit to crude. Prices will stay elevated near a $100 level without any material de-escalation emerging,” Sahdev said.The wider tensions involving Iran have also remained unresolved. US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that there was uncertainty over who was running Iran during the eight-month US-Israeli war with Iran."Their leaders are gone, their second group of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is nobody knows who the hell is running the country," Trump said.Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said on Sunday that Washington knows very well who its counterpart is in Iran and how the decision-making system in the country works.
Article Summary: WTI crude rose 1.05% to $90.38 a barrel, while Brent crude gained 1.02% to £101.60. Fresh supply concerns emerged in Saudi Arabia and the US oil and refining sector. A storm developing in the Gulf of Mexico is expected to become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days.

Article Title: Wall Street today: US stocks nears record highs amid earnings optimism, tech rally; S&P, Nasdaq rise 0.8%
Article Text:
Dow, S&P, Nasdaq rise to near record highs

Software stocks stage a comeback

US stocks moved closer to record highs on Tuesday, helped by stronger earnings expectations, easing oil prices and a renewed rally in technology shares.The S&P 500 rose 0.8 per cent and was on course to close above its previous record set in August. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 343 points, or 0.7 per cent, while the Nasdaq Composite added 0.8%, moving towards a fresh record after reaching an all-time high a day earlier.The gains have come despite continued concerns over inflation, elevated bond yields and the economic impact of the war with Iran. The S&P 500 has risen nearly 24% since hitting its low in late March.A key support for the rally has been expectations of stronger corporate profits. Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to report nearly 30% growth in earnings per share for the July-September quarter, according to FactSet. If realised, it would mark the third consecutive quarter in which earnings growth exceeded 25%.The easing in oil prices also provided some relief. Brent crude fell 1.1% to $99.19 a barrel, down from nearly $110 a few weeks ago. The decline helped push the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note down to 5.26%, from 5.31% on Monday.US software stocks have emerged as another driver of the market's recent strength, with investors increasingly betting that artificial intelligence will help rather than destroy demand for many software companies.The S&P 500 software and services index rose 1.3 per cent on Tuesday to its highest level since November 2025. The index also recorded its strongest quarterly gain since the second quarter of 2020 during the July-September period.Companies including Salesforce, ServiceNow and Accenture have reported strong results, while partnerships with AI companies have helped improve sentiment towards the sector. Cybersecurity stocks have performed particularly strongly as businesses increase spending to protect systems in the age of AI.CrowdStrike, Fortinet and Palo Alto Networks have all recorded triple-digit gains this year.“AI has been more of an enabler for a lot of these software companies, more than a disruptor,” said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist at LPL Financial.The software index is up about 5% this year, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has surged 87.5%, although chip stocks have pulled back from their highs. Meanwhile, expectations for software-sector earnings growth in 2026 have climbed to 20.6%, from 13.8% at the end of March, according to LSEG data.Software stocks suffered a sharp selloff earlier this year, with the sector falling more than 26% from late January to its April low. The decline was driven by fears that companies could use AI to develop software internally at a much lower cost, threatening traditional software providers.Those concerns now appear to have eased as companies report continued demand and greater adoption of AI tools.“The whole SaaSpocalypse didn't happen anywhere near as fast as some of the people on Wall Street thought it would,” said Rebecca Wettemann, CEO of technology research firm Valoir.However, analysts warn that AI remains a longer-term risk for the industry. Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, said the more significant test for software companies could come in the second half of 2027, when greater data-centre capacity could make AI-powered coding a bigger challenge for traditional software businesses.Additionallly, several major companies are due to report results in the coming days. Delta Air Lines is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Friday, followed by several major US banks next week.In overseas markets, European stocks edged higher as investors continued to monitor government debt and bond yields. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.1%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng gained 1%, while South Korea's Kospi fell 0.9%.
Article Summary: S&P 500 rose 0.8% and was on course to close above its previous record. Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 343 points, or 0.7%. Nasdaq Composite added 0. 8%, moving towards a fresh record. Gains come despite continued concerns over inflation, elevated bond yields and the economic impact of the war with Iran.

Article Title: Fueling both sides? South Korea ships 150,000T fuel to Russia while funding Ukraine
Article Text:
South Korea ships 150,000 tonnes fuel to Russia while funding Ukraine

Three sanctioned tankers sail to Russia

Russia turns to import fuel

South Korea is backing Ukraine, but its fuel tankers are sailing in the opposite direction — towards Russia.In July and August, more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mainly diesel, was shipped from South Korea to Russia as Moscow turned to imports to make up for falling domestic fuel production.The fuel was loaded at several South Korean ports and carried to Russia’s far east in 14 voyages by seven tankers, according to an analysis of port records and ship-tracking data by The Guardian. Three of the vessels were under UK and European Union sanctions.One sanctioned tanker received about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from another vessel in a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters. Such transfers can make cargo origins harder to trace and allow ships to avoid port terminals.The largest carrier was the sanctioned Layla, which made two trips from Ulsan in south-eastern South Korea to Vladivostok on 19 July and 10 August, carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total.On its first trip, Layla told South Korean authorities it was heading to Vladivostok. On the second, it declared Niigata in Japan as its destination before sailing to Vladivostok.The Russian-flagged Astoria, also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August.It declared Japan as its destination before sailing to Vladivostok.The third sanctioned tanker, Chongchon, did not berth at a port. Instead, it took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from the unsanctioned Celeste I at an anchorage off Yeosu in southern South Korea in early August. It then sailed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination.The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment. South Korean port records do not show who owned or sold the fuel.The shipments come as Ukrainian drone strikes disrupt Russia’s oil-refining capacity.The International Energy Agency said Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years. Diesel production was nearly 30% lower than a year earlier.Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, has said Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea in August, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. That was more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.South Korea supplied 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of the total, second only to India.Kpler data showed that buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is under UK, US, EU and Australian sanctions. NNK, a Russian oil group, was also among the buyers. Its owner, Eduard Khudainatov, and NNK-Oil are under UK sanctions.South Korea balances Ukraine support with Russia tiesThe fuel trade comes despite South Korea’s support for Ukraine. Seoul has provided humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies, including helmets, body armour and demining vehicles. In 2023, it pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans.President Lee Jae Myung also pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a Nato summit in Turkey.But Seoul has also sought to maintain ties with Russia. Throughout the war, it has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its policy of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war.Moscow has also shown interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.The fuel shipments involve vessels sanctioned by some of South Korea’s western partners but do not appear to breach South Korean law. Seoul’s measures against Russia mainly focus on export controls covering goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.The shipments come as relations between Seoul and Kyiv face strain over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul has said was meant to remain secret.Seoul defends its export controlsFuel loadings at South Korean ports began to rise sharply in July, around the time Lee pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction.A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean companies that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to restarting trade.In March, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver after the war with Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz.On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG, which will take effect in January 2027.South Korea’s foreign ministry did not directly address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”The ministry said that it had expanded export controls on Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them.The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said.
Article Summary: More than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mainly diesel, was shipped from South Korea to Russia. Moscow turned to imports to make up for falling domestic fuel production. Fuel was loaded at several South Korean ports and carried to Russia’s far east in 14 voyages by seven tankers. Three of the vessels were under UK and EU sanctions.

Article Title: Google nears $1 billion-plus nuclear power deal with Constellation amid AI boom
Article Text:
Google to seal $1 billion-plus nuclear power

Why tech cos are turning to nuclear power?

Google is close to striking a deal to buy nuclear power from Constellation Energy Corp, for its data centres, as tech gaints look for more reliable electricity to support the rapid growth of artificial intelligence.The Alphabet Inc. company could pay $1 billion or more under a multi-year agreement with Constellation, according to people familiar with the talks, as cited by Bloomberg. The deal could be announced as soon as this week. The people asked not to be named because the discussions are private.The possible deal would add to the company's already existing agreements with nuclear power companies. Last year, Google agreed to buy electricity from NextEra Energy Inc. The deal will support the company's plans to restart the Duane Arnold reactor in Iowa, which has been shut since 2020.Google also reached an agreement with Southern Co. last month for new nuclear capacity by funding upgrades at two nuclear plants. The tech firm's talks with Constellation come as technology companies face rising electricity needs from the artificial intelligence boom and growing data-centre demand.Nuclear power can provide electricity around the clock and does not produce emissions. Recent deals have mainly focused on existing nuclear plants because building new reactors can take a decade or more, including the time needed for permits and construction.The next generation of nuclear technology is also still expected to be years away from being widely deployed.Amazon.com Inc. agreed last week to buy 690 megawatts of power from Constellation. The deal includes capacity from an upgrade to the Calvert Cliffs nuclear facility in Maryland, Bloomberg reported.Microsoft Corp. agreed in 2024 to buy power from the shut Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, where Constellation is planning to restart the reactor by next year.Nuclear energy has gained interest again in recent years after safety concerns and high costs reduced interest in it earlier last decade.Growing demand for electricity from data centres has also increased interest in nuclear power. Apart from companies, many countries are also turning to nuclear energy to meet rising power demand while reducing emissions.
Article Summary: Google is close to striking a deal to buy nuclear power from Constellation Energy Corp, for its data centres. The company could pay $1 billion or more under a multi-year agreement with Constellation, according to people familiar with the talks. The deal could be announced as soon as this week.

Article Title: Oil prices hover near $100 as Middle East supply holds up, Gulf risks persist
Article Text:
Houthi attacks keep Gulf supply risks alive

Supply squeeze could last

Demand recovery may take longer

Oil prices remained close to $100 a barrel on Tuesday, with steady Middle Eastern oil exports helping to ease supply concerns. However, continued attacks in the region kept traders alert to the risk of disruptions to Gulf supplies.Brent crude was trading at $100.6 a barrel, up 24 cents or 0.24%, while WTI stood at $89.60, gaining 17 cents or 0.19%.The benchmarks have eased from around $103 a barrel after shipping data showed Middle Eastern crude exports had exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September. Oil shipments held up despite attacks on vessels travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.The supply picture also improved after G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves. The group also pledged not to restrict energy exports following pressure from US President Donald Trump.But the stronger oil flows have not removed concerns about future supplies, with fresh attacks adding to uncertainty over Gulf shipments.Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said on Monday that they had attacked several sites in Saudi Arabia, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh and Abha airport.Saudi Arabia had not immediately confirmed the attacks.The attacks came as US-Iran talks remained at a stalemate, while the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces continued to raise concerns about possible disruptions to supplies from Saudi Arabia, the region's largest oil exporter."Without a clear diplomatic breakthrough or a further material improvement in export efficiency, the floor under prices looks reasonably firm," Waterer said.The concerns around supply could persist well beyond the immediate crisis. Oil industry executives at a conference in London on Monday said shipping bottlenecks, deep cuts in refinery output and inventory withdrawals that could take years to replace could keep global oil prices high beyond this year.The Strait of Hormuz has been a major source of disruption since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran at the end of February, when Iran effectively closed the waterway and choked exports through the crucial shipping route.The disruption has been compounded by attacks on oil and gas infrastructure, which have hampered production and affected exports of crude oil and refined fuels."I think it is going to be bedlam for the bulk of the end of the year and maybe 2027," Petronas CEO Tengku Muhammad Taufik said.Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said it could take up to two years to rebuild global oil stockpiles that have been drawn down as an emergency measure.Speaking at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London in his first conference address since the start of the Iran war, Nasser said the scale of the stockpile withdrawals would make replenishment a long process."Until Hormuz fully re-opens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify. Even then, replenishing inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years," he said.Nasser said 3 billion barrels had been lost since the start of the conflict, while 1 billion barrels had been withdrawn from global inventories. The reference to both ends of the barrel covers unrefined crude as well as refined products such as diesel and jet fuel.The supply disruption could also affect the timeline for a recovery in global oil demand.ConocoPhillips Executive Chair Ryan Lance said demand could take until 2028 or 2029 to recover from this year's decline, although he expects it to grow after that.Lance said the floor for US benchmark WTI crude would rise to around $70 a barrel, with a mid-cycle price of $65 to $70 a barrel.US oil production could exceed 14 million to 14.5 million barrels per day if prices remain strong, he said, although he did not specify what he meant by strong prices.Brent futures had traded just above $100 a barrel on Monday, while WTI was close to $90, keeping both benchmarks elevated as traders balanced stronger Middle Eastern exports against the continuing risk of supply disruptions.
Article Summary: Brent crude was trading at $100.6 a barrel, up 24 cents or 0.24%, while WTI stood at $89.60. The benchmarks have eased from around $103 a barrel after shipping data showed Middle Eastern crude exports had exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September.

Article Title: Trump signs order to ease diesel costs, ‘save millions of dollars’ for farmers
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump

Diesel still costs well above last year

Trump drops diesel export ban

US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) signed an executive order aimed to ease the burden of high diesel prices on farmers, truckers and other businesses, as fuel costs continue to put pressure on Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections.Trump announced the move during a campaign stop in Grand Island, Nebraska, saying that loosening limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel would save farmers “millions” and help bring down the cost of goods and groceries.“Pete and Jim, this should absolutely ensure your election, I guarantee you that,” Trump said, addressing Republican governor Pete Ricketts and governor Jim Pillen.The order directs states to increase the availability of tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is used in farming, construction and other industries. It also calls on states to consider waiving certain fuel taxes and includes so-called non-enforcement of dyed diesel limitations.Red-dyed diesel is exempt from federal and state excise taxes. The administration says that temporarily easing restrictions would reduce costs for businesses that depend on diesel.“The typical trucker will save more than $100 every time they fill up,” Trump said as he signed the order before a crowd in Grand Island.“Farmers will also save millions and millions of dollars, and this order will also drive down the cost of all goods and to go to grocery prices very substantially.”The steps also include the treasury department reviewing certain taxes on diesel.Ten states accounting for roughly a third of US diesel sales had already taken steps to allow wider use of dyed diesel by Friday, according to research firm ClearView Energy Partners, cited by Politico. Several states had also waived taxes on diesel used in agricultural vehicles.The move comes as diesel prices remain sharply higher than a year ago.The average price of diesel fell to $6.32 a gallon on Monday, down 13 cents from the previous week but still $2.63 higher than a year ago, according to AAA.Fuel prices have surged amid the ongoing war against Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. The conflicts have contributed to a significant decline in the amount of diesel available on the global market.Exports of American diesel have also risen to record levels since the US and Israel launched a war with Iran in February and Ukraine began targeting Russian refineries.The red-dyed diesel measure follows weeks of uncertainty over how the administration would respond to rising fuel prices.Trump had repeatedly backed an outright ban on diesel exports as agriculture-state Republicans, including Iowa Senator Chuck Grassley, pushed for action to lower costs for farmers.Energy secretary Chris Wright and White House energy advisers had been working on alternatives.But on Friday, Trump ruled out a diesel export ban and said he had never really considered one, after Europe agreed to release fuel from its diesel reserves.Agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins said Monday morning that Trump would announce additional short-term relief for farmers in Nebraska and that she would also discuss the issue during a stop in Iowa.High fuel and grocery prices have become a major concern for rural voters, many of whom have backed Trump and Republicans in recent elections. Nebraska farmers and ranchers have also been angered by the administration's plan to allow more imports of foreign beef.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed to ease the burden of high diesel prices on farmers, truckers and other businesses. The order directs states to increase the availability of tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is used in farming, construction and other industries. It also calls on states to consider waiving certain fuel taxes.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
Article Summary: The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023. India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year. The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion.

Article Title: Startups Revolutionizing Carbon Dioxide into Valuable Products
Article Text: For most perfume makers, ingredients to make it smell great are the most important feature. But for Stafford Sheehan, a cofounder and chemist at Air Company, the most important part of perfume-making has no scent at all.New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. While the pale yellow-color Air Eau de Parfum is about 50% more expensive than Coco Chanel’s signature No. 5, Sheehan says his product is uniquely valuable: Every 50-milliliter bottle uses 3.6 grams of CO2 that otherwise would have been released into the atmosphere. Its package reads: “Turning CO2 into something beautiful.”While the volume of CO2 utilized in the bottle is extremely small, Air Company’s perfume showcases one way the coming wave of captured carbon can be put to use. Renewable energy and electric cars alone won’t be enough to cut CO2 emissions to zero. The world will almost certainly need to capture billions of tons of the gas annually in the coming decades. Large amounts will likely be stored underground.Using it — so-called carbon capture and utilization, or CCU — to create new products from perfume to jet fuel could be an important tool in the fight against climate change, too, though the nascent industry has major hurdles to overcome.Roughly 230 million tons of CO2 are utilized every year, according to a 2019 report by the International Energy Agency. While roughly one-third of that is reused to force more oil from the ground — hardly a carbon-neutral process — CCU advocates say that the number of companies coming up with new uses for carbon has mushroomed in recent years, paving a way to unlock climate benefits. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology and lower costs.Calgary-based CleanO2 transforms CO2 captured from building heating boilers into feedstock to make soap. Newlight Technologies, a biotechnology startup based in California, takes carbon pulled directly from the air and turns it into biodegradable plastics. Germany’s Covestro AG, one of the world’s largest polymer manufacturers, is also switching some of its fossil fuel-based feedstocks to carbon-derived materials for everything ranging from car shells to medical devices and stadium roofs.Most companies working on CO2-sequestering products are still in their infancy. To grow the emerging sector, global venture capitalists in 2022 poured nearly $500 million into carbon utilization businesses, according to the IEA. That’s in stark contrast to 2015, when barely any venture money went to technologies that utilize CO2.“It’s just a whole different landscape today than it was a decade ago,” says Sasha Mackler, executive director of the energy program at Washington, DC-based non-profit Bipartisan Policy Center.Jennifer Holmgren, chief executive officer of LanzaTech Global Inc., has experienced the shifting sentiment firsthand. The Illinois-based company uses a carbon-eating bacteria – discovered in the guts of rabbits and preserved as powder – to make alternative ethanol in bioreactors not dissimilar to how breweries ferment beer. In the early 2010s, when Holmgren touted carbon-derived ethanol to prospective customers, her sales pitch was met with skepticism.But the tide began turning later that decade. In 2018, the company’s jet fuel produced from the emissions of a Chinese steel mill helped power a Transatlantic flight. LanzaTech has also inked agreements with airlines including Japan’s All Nippon Airways to supply CO2-derived jet fuel. And LanzaJet, the company’s spin-off, plans to start producing sustainable jet fuels at a commercial scale this year.Yet for all the hype around sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using captured carbon, the industry is still an extremely small player. Almost every major airline in the world has pledged to use at least 10% sustainable jet fuels by 2030, yet SAF makes up only 0.1% of global aviation fuel supply — and much of it is made from sources other than captured CO2, such as used cooking oil.“There’s a lot more interest because consumers have become much more interested in buying things that are lower carbon,” says Holmgren. That’s enabled LanzaTech to expand the number of products that utilize CO2.American plastic container maker Plastipak, for instance, has partnered with LanzaTech to produce carbon-derived packaging materials, while polyester converted from LanzaTech’s ethanol has replaced its petroleum-based counterpart at a pilot scale in Lululemon shorts, Zara dresses, H&M yoga pants, On running shoes and Craghoppers jackets. Like SAF, though, there’s still a long way to go for CO2-derived polyester to reach meaningful levels of use.Momentum to grow beyond one-off products and low-scale production has also been supercharged by a growing array of regulations and incentives around the world. For instance, the Inflation Reduction Act that US President Joe Biden signed in 2022 raised the tax credit for carbon capture and utilization by more than 70% to $60 per metric ton in an effort to make costly projects more financially appealing.To keep the climate within habitable limits, the IEA estimates that carbon capture will have to grow to 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually by mid-century. CCU will play a role, though just how big remains to be seen. Not every use case is created equal and some approaches, such as dissolving compressed CO2 in water to make carbonated beverages, only store the gas temporarily. To quantify the true climate benefit of carbon utilization, experts say third-party verification is badly needed.The rise of CCU technology comes as another key approach in President Biden’s net-zero roadmap is hitting a bit of a wall. Carbon capture and storage — that is, gathering CO2 as it’s released from a coal-fired power plant or other emissions source and sequestering it underground — has faced challenges because carbon is often captured in one place and stored in another. That requires pipelines to transport the gas, which many local communities have opposed. Blackrock-backed Navigator, for example, recently announced it was scrapping a planned 1,300-mile CO2 pipeline.Carbon utilization companies say that they can sidestep that issue by using carbon near or at where it’s captured.At its 12-acre factory in Brooklyn, Glenwood Mason Supply demonstrates how. The concrete manufacturer takes CO2 captured at a residential building by its partner company, CarbonQuest, and uses a technique licensed from low-carbon concrete startup CarbonCure to convert the compressed carbon into a powder not unlike dry ice. It then injects it into industrial mixers. There, the CO2 meets cement, sand and aggregate, setting off a series of chemical reactions. The final result is concrete blocks with CO2 sealed in.The technique not only stores carbon but it can also make the blocks marginally stronger. The company estimates that it has utilized about 100 tons of CO2 in total since 2020. Even if the blocks break down, the stored carbon won’t be released as CO2 because it’s been mineralized.“Cement is a big offender in carbon emissions,” says Constance Cincotta, founder of the concrete factory. She became intrigued by the technology and its ability to lower her company's climate impact after hearing about it at an industry conference in the early 2010s. But it wasn't until CarbonCure came on the scene a few years ago that the prospect of CO2-storing cement became tangible. Glenwood Mason then sourced CO2 locally from CarbonQuest, which captures carbon from buildings in New York. Those factors have enabled large-scale production.While Cincotta’s intended to help the planet, she and her team discovered that sinking CO2 into concrete blocks is good for the business, too. In 2019, New York City — where the majority of the company’s concrete blocks are sold — passed a regulation requiring all buildings to shrink their carbon footprint 40% by the end of the decade. Glenwood Mason’s phones have been ringing ever since, with calls from architects and property developers who want to leverage their lower-carbon building materials to cut emissions, says Jeff Hansen, the company’s vice president in architectural sales and marketing.The factory’s CO2-storing concrete blocks also caught the eye of Amazon.com Inc, which in 2022 persuaded a real estate developer to purchase roughly 50,000 blocks for the construction of a new warehouse in New York that Amazon has leased. Had Glenwood Mason not sealed CO2 in its blocks, it wouldn’t have won the contract, Hansen says. To figure out how to pack more carbon into its products, the company has set up a laboratory in its factory to test the reaction between CO2 and other concrete feedstocks under different temperatures and humidity levels.But figuring out the right formula is only one consideration. Utilizing CO2 often comes with an additional cost. As the demand for CO2-derived products climbs, that green premium is expected to go down. Yet “it’s very hard to be a cost parity with a 100-year-old industry that doesn’t even have to pay for its externalities,” says Holmgren of LanzaTech. Even with economies of scale, Holmgren estimates that carbon-containing fabrics will still likely cost as much as 20% higher than conventional ones.“It’s unlikely that we will ever be a cost parity,” she says.In addition to the cost barrier, CCU companies also have to convince end users that may be suspicious of unproven new technologies.Changing feedstocks “does come with risks,” says Keith Wiggins, chief executive officer of Econic Technologies, a British startup that specializes in making carbon-derived chemicals. To get risk-averse industries onboard, Wiggins says his company is laser-focused on those that are under consumer pressure to change course.That strategy seems to be working. Econic has teamed up with three manufacturers in the US, China and India to produce mattresses, outdoor garments and building insulation materials that utilize CO2. The first batch of products using the company’s technology are scheduled to enter the market in 2024.For all the promise of the carbon utilization industry, it remains to be seen if it can challenge the status quo. While Air Company started selling carbon-derived perfume in 2021, the startup has yet to build its first commercial plant, Sheehan says, citing the time-consuming process needed for collecting data and fine-tuning the technology for large-scale production.Fow now, the company’s demonstration facility in New York City — where CO2 and hydrogen gas flow through tubes into a reactor to form chemical reactions, aided by catalysts made from a confidential mixture of metals — is designed to yield at least 10,000 gallons of CO2-derived liquid annually. The limited production capacity has left many orders for its perfume — as well as jet fuels and Air Vodka, another popular product made from CO2 — unfilled.“We need to scale these facilities to the size of oil refineries today in order to have the impact on climate change that we want to have,” Sheehan says.
Article Summary: New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology.

Article Title: E-commerce firm Udaan raises $340 million ahead of planned IPO
Article Text: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain and boost vendor partnerships ahead of a stock market debut planned for 2025.The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt, the Bangalore-based company said in a statement Thursday. The round was led by M&G Plc and existing investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and DST Global participated.The round “fully funds our business plan,” Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan co-founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. “It enables our continued journey of growth and profitability, positioning us well to be public-market ready in the next 12-18 months.”Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, runs an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business, though a very small part of India’s overall retail market, is expected to swell to $150 billion in sales in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co.The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas, Gupta told Bloomberg News last month.Udaan was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran the company until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.
Article Summary: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain. The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt. The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas.

Article Title: Minuscule AI startup raises $41 million to tap India growth
Article Text: A generative artificial intelligence startup targeting the Indian market raised $41 million in fresh funding, the largest such round by an early-stage AI contender in the country.Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages at price points that the country’s 1.4 billion people can afford. The Series A funding round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, and participants included Silicon Valley billionaire Vinod Khosla’s Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners, formerly Sequoia Capital India & Southeast Asia, Sarvam said Thursday.The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems as well as tools for creating apps for the meager compute infrastructure available to developers in India. The startup has a total of 18 employees and is just opening an office in the city."What we are showing is that you can build large language models with limited resources,” Raghavan said in a phone interview. "We are building at a smaller scale and demonstrating that these can be extremely cost and energy efficient so they can be accessed by everyone."Large language models, like OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama, are powerful AI systems that understand by learning from vast amounts of diverse data from the internet and elsewhere to summarize, translate, and create text, audio and video for a wide range of applications. The rivalry to develop ever-more sophisticated models is heating up in Silicon Valley and such efforts have attracted billions of dollars in investments.
Article Summary: Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages. The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co- founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems.

Article Title: ZestMoney set to shut operations this month
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Buy now Pay Later (BNPL) startup ZestMoney has decided to shut operations. The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. ZestMoney did not comment. It is learnt that the firm will shut down by the end of this month.The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The deal was called off earlier this year after a due diligence process undertaken by PhonePe, while evaluating the potential acquisition failed to meet its bar. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.

The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.
